'''Tommaso Ceva''' (December 20, 1648 &ndash; February 3, 1737) was an Italian [[Jesuit]] [[mathematician]] from [[Milan]].  He was the brother of [[Giovanni Ceva]]. His work aided in spreading a knowledge of [[Isaac Newton|Newton]]'s discovery of the [[Newton's law of universal gravitation|law of gravitation]].

== Biography ==
Tommaso Ceva was born into a wealthy Milanese family in 1648. After studying at the Collegio di Brera, a Jesuit college in Milan, on 24 March 1663 he entered the [[Jesuits|Society of Jesus]]. He taught mathematics and [[rhetoric]] at the Jesuit College of Brera in Milan for thirty-eight years.<ref>{{cite book|title=The Jesuits and Italian Universities, 1548-1773|page=379|first=Paul F.|last=Grendler|year=2017|publisher=[[CUA Press]]|language=en|isbn=9780813229362}}</ref> His most famous student was [[Giovanni Girolamo Saccheri]]. Under the tutelage of Ceva, Saccheri wrote his first work, titled ''Quaesita geometrica'' (Geometric Investigations, 1693). Ceva was one of the main representatives of [[Clelia Grillo Borromeo]]'s Academia Vigilantium.{{sfn|Gronda|1980}} [[Joseph I, Holy Roman Emperor|Joseph I]] named him Caesarian Theologian early in the 18th century.{{sfn|Gronda|1980}}

His first scientific work, ''De natura gravium'' (The Nature of Gravity, 1699), dealt with physical subjects - such as [[gravity]] and [[free fall]] - in a philosophical way. His only mathematical work, published in 1699 was the ''Opuscula Mathematica'' (Mathematical Essays), which dealt with [[geometry]], gravity and [[arithmetic]]. Ceva designed an instrument to divide a [[right angle]] into a specified number of equal parts.<ref>''Instrumentum pro sectione cujuscunque anguli rectilinei in partes quotcunque aequales'' (Milan, 1695; repr. In ''Acta eruditorum'' [1695], p. 290).</ref> His device, described in the ''[[Acta Eruditorum]]'' in 1695, won him the attention of [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz|Leibniz]].<ref>{{cite book|title=The Sun in the Church. Cathedrals as Solar Observatories|author-link=John L. Heilbron|first=John L.|last=Heilbron|year=2009|isbn=9780674038486|page=213|publisher=[[Harvard University Press]]}}</ref> This same instrument was described in 1704 by the [[France|French]] [[mathematician]] [[Guillaume de l'Hôpital]].{{sfn|Oettel|1981|page=183}}

In his ''Philosophia novo-antiqua'' (New-Ancient Philosophy, 1704) Ceva defended [[scholasticism]] against the systems [[René Descartes|Descartes]] and [[Pierre Gassendi|Gassendi]] and tried to reconcile the best of ancient and modern [[natural philosophy]].{{sfn|Lindon|2002}} The work comprises six dissertations, dealing with topics ranging from mathematics to [[cosmology]] and [[mechanics]], and engages with live issues for the science of the time ([[Copernican heliocentrism|Copernican theory]]; Descartes's physics and denial of animal souls; Gassendi's [[atomism]]). Ceva accepted Galileo's theory of motion but not his cosmology. As far as [[Cartesian physics]] is concerned, he especially criticized the identification of the [[essence]] of [[matter]] with [[Res extensa|extension]].<ref>{{cite book
 |chapter= "Italy Did Not Want to Be Cartesian" And For Good Reason
 |title= The Oxford Handbook of Descartes and Cartesianism
 |year= 2019
 |last= Belgioioso
 |first= Giulia
 |publisher= [[Oxford University Press]]
 |location= New York
 |page= 527
 |isbn= 978-0192517210
}}</ref> Ceva's ''Philosophia novo-antiqua'' was reissued in Wien in 1719, in Florence in 1723 and in Venice in 1732.

Ceva was also a noted [[poet]] and dedicated a significant amount of his time to this task. In the literary field Ceva shared the Arcadian reaction against [[marinism]], and summed it up in his oft-quoted definition of poetry as ‘un sogno che si fa in presenza della ragione’ (“a dream made in the presence of reason”).{{sfn|Lindon|2002}} His Latin poem ''Jesus Puer'', dedicated to the Holy Roman emperor [[Joseph I, Holy Roman Emperor|Joseph I]], was translated into many languages including [[German language|German]] and [[Italian language|Italian]]. Two other collections of Latin verses, ''Sylvae'' (1699; “Woods”) and ''Carmina'' (1704; “Poems”), range over philosophic, scientific, religious, and literary subjects. Ceva was made a fellow of the [[Pontifical Academy of Arcadia|Arcadia]] in 1718 and was in correspondence with [[Vincenzo Viviani]] and [[Luigi Guido Grandi]].{{sfn|Gronda|1980}} He was a close friend of the mathematician [[Pietro Paolo Caravaggio]] and his son Pietro Paolo Caravaggio junior.{{sfn|Ulivi|1989|page=93}}

His ''Opuscula mathematica'' brought him international fame and his ''Carmina'' were favourably reviewed in ''[[Acta Eruditorum]]''.<ref>''Actorum eruditorum quae Lipsiae publicantur. Supplementa'' 3 (1702): 423–5.</ref> His work was highly praised by [[Gotthold Ephraim Lessing]] and [[Christian Friedrich Daniel Schubart]].{{sfn|Oettel|1981|page=184}}

In his latter years, Ceva suffered from [[paralysis]]. He died in Milan on 3 February 1737.{{sfn|Gronda|1980}} The 6,5-kilometer sized main-belt asteroid [[12579 Ceva]], discovered at the [[San Vittore Observatory]] in 1999, was named in honor of him and his brother, Giovanni.<ref>{{cite book
  |title = Dictionary of Minor Planet Names |publisher = Springer Berlin Heidelberg
  |page  = 786
  |date  = 2007
  |isbn  = 978-3-540-00238-3
  |doi   = 10.1007/978-3-540-29925-7_8648 |chapter = (12579) Ceva }}</ref>

== The Cycloid of Ceva ==
[[File:Cycloid of ceva.gif|thumb|Cycloid of Ceva]]
Prompted by the familiar "insertion" method of [[Archimedes]], Ceva devised in 1699 a curve for [[Angle trisection|trisection]] which was called the "Cycloidum anomalarum".<ref>{{MathWorld |title=Cycloid of Ceva |id=CycloidofCeva}}</ref> The principle involved is that of doubling angles. The cycloid of Ceva has the [[polar equation]]

:<math>r=1+2\cos(2\theta)</math>.

In [[Cartesian coordinate]]s the equation of this curve is
:<math>(x^2+y^2)^3=(3x^2-y^2)^2</math>.

To trisect the angle <math>\angle ABC </math>, construct a line parallel to the polar axis (the positive <math>x</math> axis). Let <math>D</math> be the point of intersection of the cycloid and the line. Then the angle <math>\angle ABD </math> is one-third of the angle <math>\angle ABC </math>.

Proof: let angle <math>\angle ABD </math> be <math> \theta</math> and let the point <math>F</math> on the <math>x</math> axis be such that <math>|BE| = |EF| = 1</math>. Let <math>G</math> be the [[orthogonal projection]] of <math>F</math> on the line <math>BD</math>. The angle <math>\angle DEF = 2\theta</math>, so <math>|BG| = 1 +\cos(2\theta)</math>. Since <math>|BD| = 1 + 2\cos(2\theta)</math>, <math>|EG| = |GD|</math>, <math>|DF| = |EF| = 1</math>. So angle <math>\angle DFH </math> equals <math>4\theta-\angle EFA=3\theta</math>, but <math>\angle DFH=\angle CBA </math>.
